svg.aria-label: A real tail loss probe: the Pi resends its last segment after 65 ms of silence, and the server later reports the duplicate with a D-SACK

g.text: 33.5 ms: the first part of a TLS hello (Chapter 32)
the rest: the last thing the Pi has to send
113.2 ms: it had everything all along
189.0 ms: “by the way, I got those bytes twice”

ol.li: The Pi sends the two segments of a TLS hello, and then has nothing more to send until the server answers.

Normally, a lost segment is noticed when later segments arrive and the receiver sends duplicate ACKs. But when the lost one is the last, nothing follows it, so nothing reveals the loss, and the sender would have to wait for its full timeout (at least 200 ms on Linux, often much more). So Linux uses a tail loss probe: after about two round trips of silence, it resends the last segment, to provoke an acknowledgement.
Here, nothing had been lost: the server’s acknowledgement was just slow, and crossed the probe on the way.

The server’s next acknowledgement carries a D-SACK (“duplicate SACK”): a SACK block for bytes before the acknowledgement number, which means “these arrived twice”. Now the Pi knows its resend was unnecessary, and that the network didn’t really lose anything. That matters for the next chapter: TCP slows down when it thinks it’s lost data, and a D-SACK lets it undo that.

figure.figcaption: Lost, or just slow? Three unnecessary resends in this capture, and how TCP found out.
